help.combat.body:
## Battles

A battle starts when fleets of players who are enemies meet at the same place and at least one of them is armed
and willing to attack. Battles are fought on a small grid over several rounds. Each round, ships move in order of
their initiative, and weapons fire at targets in range: beams lose strength over distance, torpedoes can miss.
Shields absorb damage before armor; a ship whose armor is gone is destroyed.

## Battle plans

A battle plan tells a fleet what to shoot first, which secondary targets to accept, how to fight (for example, to
close in, to keep its distance, or to run away) and whom to attack. Edit your plans with {key:battle_plans} (or
**Commands > Battle Plans**) and pick a fleet's plan in its Battle plan tile.

## Who is an enemy

Player relations decide whom your fleets fight. Open them with {key:relations} (or **Commands > Player Relations**)
and mark each player as a friend, neutral or an enemy. See [[relations]].

## Watching a battle

After a battle you get a message about it. The battle viewer replays it round by round, and the battle report
lists every battle you took part in this year.

## Bombing and invasion

Fleets with bombs over an enemy planet bomb it each year, killing colonists and destroying installations; the
planet's defenses shoot some of the bombs down. Ships carrying colonists can invade an enemy planet by unloading
them there: your troops fight the planet's defenders, and if they win, the planet is yours.

help.design.body:
Open the designer with {key:ship_design} (or **Commands > Ship Design**). It has three lists: your ship designs,
your starbase designs, and the hulls and parts you could use.

## Making a design

- Pick a hull. Its slots appear in the picture; each slot takes certain kinds of parts and holds up to a number of
  them.
- Choose **Copy** with a hull selected to start a new design on it, or with a design selected to start from
  that design.
- Drag parts from the list into the slots, or double-click a part to put it in the first slot that takes it.
  Drag a part out of a slot, or right-click it, to take it out. Some slots must be filled, such as a ship's
  engine slots.
- The totals beside the picture show the design's cost, mass, armor, shields, speed, fuel, cargo and weapons as
  you go.
- Name the design and choose **OK**. It can then be built at any planet that can build it.

New hulls and parts become available as your tech levels rise (see [[research]]). Some parts only exist for races
with certain traits (see [[races]]).

## Ships and starbases

Starbases are designed the same way, from starbase hulls, and are built by the planet they will orbit. A starbase
with a dock can build ships; a larger dock can build larger ships.

## Changing a design

**Edit** changes a design. A design with ships flying can't be changed: copy it and change the copy instead.
**Delete** removes a design, and every ship built to it goes with it, so be careful.
help.design.title: Ship design
help.fleets.body:
Ships fly in fleets. A fleet has a list of waypoints: waypoint 0 is where it is now, and each later waypoint is a
place to go, with the warp speed to fly there and a task to do on arrival.

## Moving

- Select a fleet and Shift-click on the map to add waypoints (see [[scanner]]).
- In the Waypoints tile, pick a waypoint to change its speed and task, or press **Delete** to remove it.
- Higher warp is faster but burns much more fuel. The tile shows the distance, the years it will take and the fuel
  you will have left; it warns you when the fleet will run out of fuel on the way.
- Fleets refuel at your planets' starbases, and some engines scoop fuel as they fly.
- Flying faster than warp 9 can damage ships that aren't built for it.

## Tasks

- **Transport:** load or unload cargo (minerals, colonists, fuel). The quick choices load or drop everything, or
  wait until the hold is full.
- **Colonize:** settle the planet with the colonists aboard a ship that has a colonization module.
- **Remote mining:** mine an uninhabited planet with a fleet that has mining robots.
- **Merge with fleet:** join another of your fleets there.
- **Scrap fleet:** take the ships apart; part of their minerals are recovered at the planet.
- **Lay mines:** lay a minefield with the fleet's mine layers.
- **Patrol:** look for enemy fleets nearby and go after them.
- **Route:** send the fleet on to the planet's route destination.
- **Transfer fleet:** give the fleet to another player.

A fleet can repeat its orders: when it reaches its last waypoint, it starts over from the first.

## Fleet tiles

- **Fleet composition:** the ships in the fleet; split ships off into new fleets, or merge fleets that are
  together.
- **Cargo:** what the fleet carries; the cargo dialog moves cargo between the fleet and a planet or another fleet
  in the same place.
- **Battle plan:** how the fleet behaves when a fight starts (see [[combat]]).
help.fleets.title: Fleets and waypoints
help.hazards.body:
## Minefields

Fleets with mine layers can lay minefields. A fleet moving through an enemy minefield may hit a mine, take damage
and be stopped; flying slowly lowers the chance. Fleets with beam weapons or mine sweepers sweep mines away. Fields
shrink a little each year.

## Stargates

Planets whose starbases have stargates can send fleets instantly to another gate, within the gates' limits on
range and ship mass. Going beyond those limits is possible but can destroy ships.

## Mass drivers and packets

A starbase with a mass driver can fling minerals at another planet as a packet. The receiving planet needs a mass
driver of its own to catch it safely; an uncaught packet hits the planet hard.

## Wormholes

Wormholes connect two points in space. A fleet that reaches one end comes out of the other. Wormholes drift, and
now and then their ends jump to new places.

## Salvage

Ships that are scrapped in space or destroyed leave salvage that fleets can pick up as cargo.

## The Mystery Trader

A strange ship that crosses the galaxy from time to time. Meet it with a fleet carrying enough minerals and it may
give you something rare in return.

## Random events

If the game allows them, comets, mineral discoveries, research breakthroughs, artifacts and other events happen now
and then.

## On the map

- **Mouse wheel:** zoom in and out.
- **Right or middle drag:** move the map.
- **Click:** select; click again to step through what is there.
- **Right-click:** a menu of what is at that spot.
- **Shift-click:** add a waypoint for the selected fleet.
- **Escape:** cancel picking a planet.

## In lists and dialogs

- **Shift** and **Ctrl** with the production and cargo buttons: 10 or 100 at a time (both together in the cargo

help.messages.body:
Each year brings messages: what your planets built, what your scanners discovered, battles, research, random
events and more. They are shown one at a time in the messages pane.

- The arrow buttons step to the previous and next message.
- **Goto** jumps to what the message is about: it selects a planet, a fleet, the Mystery Trader, a minefield or a
  packet on the map (scrolling the map to it), or opens the research window, the designer, the battle viewer or the
  score.
- The box by each message shows whether its kind is shown or filtered out; click it to change that for the
  rest of the game. A magnifying glass appears while any of this year's messages are filtered.

Read your messages every year: they are how you learn that a colony was founded, a fleet ran out of fuel, a
minefield was hit or an enemy appeared.

help.modes.body:
## Against the computer

Choose **New Game...** in the main menu. Pick the size of the galaxy and how many computer players to face, and how
hard they play. **Advanced Game** lets you set every option: density, starting positions, victory conditions, each
computer player's personality and difficulty, and other human players.

## Hotseat

Several people take turns at one computer. Add human players in **Advanced Game**. When one player's orders are in,
a cover hides the screen until the next player is ready, so nobody sees another's turn. The year is generated when
everyone has finished.

## Play by email

One person hosts the game and generates the turns; the others play from **turn files**.

- The host creates the game with the host tool and sends each player their turn file.
- Each player opens their turn file from the main menu (**Open Turn File**), gives orders and submits them, which
  writes an orders file to send back to the host.
- The host generates the next year once the orders are in, and sends out the new turn files.

A turn file holds only what that player knows; it can't be used to peek at others.

## Saving

**File > Save** ({key:save}) saves the whole game, including its computer players, so you can stop and carry on
later from **Open Game** in the main menu.
help.modes.title: Ways to play
help.mods.body:
The game can be changed with mods: new parts and hulls, changed rules, new events, other looks and wording. Open
**Mods...** in the main menu to turn mods on or off and to set their order.

- **Gameplay mods** change the rules. Every player in a game needs the same ones, so a saved game remembers which
  were on and turns them on again when it's loaded.
- **Cosmetic mods** change only what you see: pictures, text and fonts. Each player can choose their own.
- A mod with scripts asks for your trust before it runs. Only trust mods from people you trust.

Mods are folders in your user data folder, under `mods`. The game's modding guide explains how to make one.

## The classic look

If you own a copy of the original Stars!, the game can import its pictures and wording from your copy as a
cosmetic mod for your own use. Choose **Import Classic Look...** in the main menu and point it at the folder you
installed it in. Nothing is copied anywhere but your own computer, and the game plays the same with or without it.

help.planets.body:
Every planet has an environment (gravity, temperature and radiation), mineral deposits, and perhaps a population.

## Value

A planet's **value** says how well your race can live there, from your race's preferred ranges for gravity,
temperature and radiation (set in the race wizard, see [[races]]). A positive value means your colonists will
grow; the higher, the faster and the more of them the planet can hold. A negative value means the planet is
hostile: colonists there die off a little every year. Terraforming can move a planet's environment toward what
your race likes and raise its value.

## Population and growth

Colonists grow each year toward the planet's capacity. Growth slows as a planet fills up, and a planet over its
capacity loses people. Colonists are counted in hundreds; cargo holds carry them in units of 100.

## Minerals

There are three minerals: **ironium**, **boranium** and **germanium**. Each planet has a concentration of each (how
rich the deposits are) and minerals already mined lying on its surface. Mines dig minerals up each year; the richer
the deposit, the more they dig, and deposits slowly wear down as they are mined. Minerals pay, with resources, for
everything you build.

## Resources

Your colonists and your factories produce **resources** every year. Resources pay for production and research.
How many colonists run a factory, and how many resources each makes, depend on your race.

## Installations

- **Mines** dig minerals.
- **Factories** make resources.
- **Defenses** protect the planet against bombing and invasion.
- A **planetary scanner** lets the planet see fleets and planets around it.
- A **starbase** orbits the planet; it can repair ships, refuel them, build them (with a dock) and fight.

How many mines, factories and defenses a planet can run depends on its population. The planet tiles and the
summary show what a planet has and what it could have. See [[production]] to build them.
help.planets.title: Planets
help.production.body:
Each of your planets builds from its own production queue, paid with that planet's resources and the minerals on
its surface. Open it from the planet's Production tile.

## The queue

- The left list shows what the planet can build; the right list is the queue, built from the top down.
- **Add** puts the selected item into the queue; **Remove** takes it out; the arrows move an item up or down.
- Hold **Shift** to add or remove 10 at a time, and **Ctrl** for 100.
- Factories, mines and defenses can only be queued up to the number the planet can use, counting those already
  built and queued.
- The cost of the selected item and an estimate of when each item will be finished are shown below the lists. The
  estimate follows the leftover box below: with it checked, nothing is set aside for research first.

Anything the planet can't finish this year carries on next year, keeping what has been spent on it. When the
queue runs dry, leftover resources can go to research (the "contribute only leftover resources to research"
setting).

## Standing orders

Some items are **auto** items, such as Auto Mines, Auto Factories and Auto Max Terraform. They stay in the queue and
build up to the number you set each year, as long as there is something left to build, so a planet keeps growing
without you editing its queue every year.

## Ships and starbases

A planet with a starbase that has a dock can build ships; any of your planets can build or replace its starbase.
Your own designs appear in the list once you have made them in the ship designer (see [[design]]).

## Templates

The queue can be filled from a **production template**. The default template is what every new colony starts
with. You can keep a few more templates of your own and apply them to any planet.
help.production.title: Production
help.races.body:
Before a game you can design your own race in the race wizard, or play one of the ready-made races. A race is a
balance of strengths and weaknesses, paid for with **advantage points**: strong choices cost points, weak ones give
points back, and the race must not end up with fewer than zero.

## What a race is made of

- **Primary racial trait:** the race's way of life, such as long-range traders, shapeshifters or warmongers. It
  decides much about how the race plays.
- **Lesser racial traits:** smaller advantages and drawbacks, such as better engines or cheaper research.
- **Environment:** the gravity, temperature and radiation the race prefers, as ranges. Wider ranges make more
  planets worth settling; a race can also be immune to one of them.
- **Growth rate:** how fast colonists multiply.
- **Economy:** how many colonists run a factory, how many resources factories and mines produce, and what they
  cost.
- **Research costs:** cheaper or dearer for each of the six fields, with an option to start some fields at level 3.

The wizard shows the advantage points left as you change things, and how many planets your race could expect to
find habitable. Races are saved as files you can use again.
help.races.title: Races
help.relations.body:
You meet other races as your scanners find them. The **Player Relations** window ({key:relations}) lists every
race you know, and lets you set how you treat each one:

- **Friend:** your fleets don't attack theirs, and theirs can use your starbases' gates and repair.
- **Neutral:** your fleets fight theirs only if your battle plans say to attack neutrals.
- **Enemy:** your armed fleets attack theirs when they meet.

Relations are one-sided: a race you call a friend may still call you an enemy.

## Others' fleets

Fleets of other players that your scanners can see this year are drawn on the map. Click one to see its owner,
ships and mass in the summary pane. You can make a fleet follow or chase one by Shift-clicking it as a waypoint.
The **Others' Fleets** report lists all of them.

## Giving things away

A fleet's Transfer task gives the fleet to another player. Cargo can also be handed to another player's fleet or
planet.
help.relations.title: Other players
help.reports.body:
The **Report** menu opens tables of your planets, your fleets, others' fleets you have seen, and this year's
battles. Press {key:reports} to open them and again for the next one.

- Click a column's label for its menu: sort by it, forward or reverse, or hide it (or show a hidden one).
  The sort you had before becomes the second level, which breaks ties.
- Click a row to put that planet or fleet under command. Some cells do more: a planet's Production cell opens
  its production queue, and a fleet's Cargo cell opens the cargo dialog.
- In the battle report, click a battle to select where it was fought, and again to watch it.

## Score

The score window ({key:score}) ranks every player and shows a graph of how the scores have changed. The score
counts planets, population, resources, tech levels, starbases and ships.

## Winning

The game's creator picks which victory conditions count, how many of them a player must meet, and how many years
must pass before anyone can win. The conditions include owning a share of all planets, reaching a tech level in
some fields, reaching a score, being well ahead of the second player, producing enough resources, having enough
capital ships, and having the highest score after a number of years. When a player wins, every player is told.

A player who has lost all planets and all ships is eliminated.
help.reports.title: Reports and score
help.research.body:
Your race studies six fields: **energy**, **weapons**, **propulsion**, **construction**, **electronics** and
**biotechnology**. Each has a level; higher levels unlock new parts and hulls and make building them cheaper.

Open the research window with {key:research} (or **Commands > Research**).

## What you can set

- **Resources for research:** the share of every planet's resources that goes to research each year. The rest goes
  to production.
- **Current field:** the field your research goes into now.
- **Next field:** what to study once the current level is reached: a field you choose, the same field again, or
  whichever field has the lowest level.

The window shows each field's level, how much you've put toward the next level, and an estimate of how long it
will take. Fields your race is good at cost less; your race's research costs are set in the race wizard (see
[[races]]).

Leftover resources from planets with nothing left to build can also go to research (see [[production]]).
Scrapping alien ships, capturing planets and battle can sometimes teach you a level too.
help.research.title: Research
help.scanner.body:
The scanner is the map in the middle of the screen. Planets are circles; your fleets are triangles pointing toward
their next waypoint; other players' fleets are triangles in their own colour. Minefields show as faint discs, and
you may also see wormholes, mineral packets, salvage and the Mystery Trader.

## Moving around

- **Zoom:** the mouse wheel, or the zoom buttons on the toolbar.
- **Pan:** drag with the right or middle mouse button.
- **Select:** click a planet or fleet. Clicking the same spot again steps through everything there.
- **What's here:** right-click (without dragging) for a menu of the planet and every fleet at that spot.

The status bar under the map shows the position under the mouse, what is there, and how far it is from what you
have selected.

## Giving fleets orders on the map

With one of your fleets selected:

- **Shift-click** adds a waypoint after the selected one: a planet, a fleet (to follow it), a wormhole, the Mystery
  Trader, a minefield, a packet or salvage, or a point in space.
- **Drag** a waypoint to move it somewhere else.
- The fleet's path is drawn from waypoint to waypoint.

More about fleets and tasks in [[fleets]].

## Views and overlays

The toolbar above the map switches the view:

- **Normal:** planets in their owners' colours.
- **Minerals:** the minerals lying on each planet's surface.
- **Conc.:** how rich each planet's mineral deposits are.
- **Value:** how good each planet is for your race (see [[planets]]). A flag marks each planet someone lives on, in
  your colour, a friend's (yellow), a neutral's (dark red) or an enemy's (red).
- **Pop.:** population.

**Names** writes planet names next to the planets. **Scan** shows your scanner coverage: normal scanners in red,
penetrating scanners (which also see fleets in orbit and planets' contents behind them) in green.
help.scanner.title: The scanner
help.screen.body:
The screen has four panes, and most of the game is played in them.

## Command pane (left)

Tiles for the planet or fleet you have selected, in two columns. Each tile has a title bar; click its arrow to fold
the tile up or open it again. Drag a tile by its title bar onto another tile to put it there, or below a column's
tiles to put it at the bottom of that column; the game remembers where you put them. For a planet you see its
status, production, starbase and routes (hold the mouse button down on the starbase tile to see its design); for a
fleet, its ships, cargo, waypoints, the task at the selected waypoint, and its battle plan. The arrow buttons next
to the name step through your planets or fleets.

## Scanner (centre)

The map of the galaxy, as far as your scanners and records know it. See [[scanner]].

## Messages (bottom left)

This year's messages, one at a time, with buttons to step through them and to jump to what a message is about.
See [[messages]].

## Selection summary (bottom right)

A short summary of whatever is selected on the map: for a planet, its value, how old your report on it is, its
population, environment and minerals; for a fleet, its ships, fuel, cargo, mass and next waypoint. Hold the left
mouse button on a fleet's picture to see its ships, or the right button to see its main design.

## Menus

- **File:** save, close the game, quit.
- **View:** the scanner's views and overlays, and Settings (fonts, interface size, colours, keys).
- **Turn:** generate the turn (or submit your orders, in a game with other players).
- **Commands:** ship design, research, battle plans, player relations.
- **Report:** tables of your planets, your fleets and others' fleets, battles, and the score.
- **Help:** this help, and the version you are running.

Keyboard shortcuts are listed in [[keys]].
help.screen.title: The game screen
help.start.body:
StarsGodot is a turn-based game of galactic expansion. You lead one race from a single home planet. Explore the
stars around you, settle the worlds your people can live on, out-research and out-build your rivals, and win by
the goals set when the game was created.

## A year at a time

Each turn is one year. During a turn you give orders: what your planets build, where your fleets fly and what they
do when they arrive, which technology your scientists study, and how your race treats the others. Nothing happens
until the turn is generated. Then every player's orders are carried out together, in a fixed order, and you get a
new year, with messages about what happened.

- Press {key:generate} (or **Turn > Generate**) when your orders are ready.
- In a game with other human players, the year is generated once everyone has submitted. See [[modes]].

## Your first few years

- Look at your home planet in the [[planets|planet tiles]] on the left. It starts with mines, factories and a
  starbase.
- Open its production queue and keep it busy: factories and mines grow your economy; scouts find new worlds;
  colony ships settle them. See [[production]].
- Send your scout out to look at the stars nearby. Select it, then Shift-click a planet on the map to add a
  waypoint. See [[fleets]].
- Set a research field and how much of your resources goes to research. See [[research]].
- Read your messages: they report what your scanners saw, what was built and what needs your attention. See
  [[messages]].

Planets with a high value (green on the map's Value view) are where your colonists will grow best. See [[scanner]]
for the map's views.

trait.lrt.ARM.description: You get better remote mining ships and parts, and start with two mining ships.
trait.lrt.ARM.name: Advanced Remote Mining
trait.lrt.BET.description: New technology costs twice as much to build at first, but your parts get cheaper faster as your tech improves.
trait.lrt.BET.name: Bleeding Edge Technology
trait.lrt.CE.description: Engines cost you half as much, but they can fail at high warp and leave the fleet stalled. You start one level higher in Propulsion.
trait.lrt.CE.name: Cheap Engines
trait.lrt.GR.description: Half of each year's research goes to the field you chose, and a share goes to every other field at the same time.
trait.lrt.GR.name: Generalized Research
trait.lrt.IFE.description: Your engines burn 15% less fuel, and you start one level higher in Propulsion.
trait.lrt.IFE.name: Improved Fuel Efficiency
trait.lrt.ISB.description: Your starbases cost 20% less and are partly cloaked.
trait.lrt.ISB.name: Improved Starbases
trait.lrt.LSP.description: Your homeworld starts with fewer colonists.
trait.lrt.LSP.name: Low Starting Population
trait.lrt.MA.description: Mineral alchemy costs you only a quarter as much.
trait.lrt.MA.name: Mineral Alchemy
trait.lrt.NAS.description: Penetrating scanners are not available to you, but your other scanners reach twice as far.
trait.lrt.NAS.name: No Advanced Scanners
trait.lrt.NRSE.description: Ram scoop engines, which gather fuel as they fly, are not available to you.
trait.lrt.NRSE.name: No Ram Scoop Engines
trait.lrt.OBRM.description: Your planets hold 10% more colonists, but you cannot build remote mining ships.
trait.lrt.OBRM.name: Only Basic Remote Mining
trait.lrt.RS.description: Your shields regenerate during battle and are 40% stronger, but your armor is only half as strong.
trait.lrt.RS.name: Regenerating Shields
trait.lrt.TT.description: You can terraform further and for less, and terraforming research needs only Biotechnology.
trait.lrt.TT.name: Total Terraforming
trait.lrt.UR.description: Scrapping ships at your planets returns more minerals and some resources too.
trait.lrt.UR.name: Ultimate Recycling
trait.prt.AR.description: Your people live in orbit: every colony is a starbase, you build no mines, factories, defenses or planetary scanners, and your resources come from your population and Energy tech. You cannot invade planets and your ships lose a little cargo in flight, but starbases cost you less.
trait.prt.AR.name: Alternate Reality
trait.prt.CA.description: Your terraforming costs half as much and takes effect at once, and planets you lose go back to their original environment. New colonies never get auto-terraforming in their queues. You start with Biotechnology 6 and a terraforming ship.
trait.prt.CA.name: Claim Adjuster
trait.prt.HE.description: Your population grows twice as fast as other races', but each planet holds only half as many of your colonists. You start with three small colony ships to spread out early. Stargates are not available to you.
trait.prt.HE.name: Hyper-Expansion
trait.prt.IS.description: Your planetary defenses cost less and hold off invaders twice as well, your fleets and starbases repair faster, and colonists aboard your ships grow. Weapons and bombs cost you a quarter more, and the strongest bombs are not available to you.
trait.prt.IS.name: Inner-Strength
trait.prt.IT.description: Your stargates cost less and can send ships with cargo, you see other races' stargates, and you catch packets more easily. You start with Propulsion 5 and Construction 5, a stargate at home, and a second planet in larger universes.
trait.prt.IT.name: Inter-stellar Traveler
trait.prt.JoaT.description: A balanced race without a specialty: your planets hold 20% more colonists, some of your hulls carry a scanner that improves with your tech, and you start with tech 3 in every field and a varied fleet.
trait.prt.JoaT.name: Jack of All Trades
trait.prt.PP.description: Your mass drivers fling mineral packets cheaply; your packets lose less on the way, terraform the planets they reach and show you who catches them. You start with Energy 4 and a mass driver at home, and a second planet in larger universes.
trait.prt.PP.name: Packet Physics
trait.prt.SD.description: You are masters of minefields: yours decay slowly near your planets, can be laid on the move and detonated at will, your ships cross minefields faster, and you see the designs of ships your mines hit. You start with two minelayers.
trait.prt.SD.name: Space Demolition
trait.prt.SS.description: Your ships have built-in cloaking, your spies gain from other races' research, and your ships cross minefields a little faster. You start with Electronics 5 and a stealthy scout and courier.
trait.prt.SS.name: Super-Stealth
trait.prt.WM.description: Your ships move further in battle, weapons and bombs cost you a quarter less, your troops invade harder, and you see the full designs of the ships you scan. You start with Weapons 6 and armed escorts, but some planetary defenses and the smallest mine layer are not available to you.
trait.prt.WM.name: War Monger
tutorial.colonize.text:
Your **Settler** carries colonists. Switch the map to the **Value** view on the toolbar: green planets suit your race, red ones don't.

Select the Settler, Shift-click a nearby green planet, and in the **Waypoint Task** tile choose **Colonize**.
tutorial.colonize.title: A new world
tutorial.colony.text:
Keep generating years until your Settler reaches its planet and founds your first colony. Meanwhile, follow your scouts' discoveries and give them new waypoints when they arrive.

A new colony starts with its own empty production queue: give it something to build too.
tutorial.colony.title: Waiting for the colony
tutorial.done.text:
Your race has its first colony. From here on it's up to you: keep expanding to good planets, design better ships as your tech improves ({key:ship_design}), and keep an eye on your neighbour.

The help ({key:help}) covers everything this tutorial left out. Good luck!
tutorial.done.title: On your own
tutorial.generate.text: Your orders are ready. Choose **Turn > Generate** ({key:generate}): every player's orders are carried out together, and a new year begins.
tutorial.generate.title: The first year
tutorial.messages.text:
Each year brings messages, shown in the pane at the bottom left. Step through them with the arrow buttons; **Goto** takes you to what a message is about.

Read them every year: they tell you what was built, what your scanners found, and what needs your attention.

Choose **Next** when you've had a look.
tutorial.messages.title: News from your empire
tutorial.queue.text:
A planet builds only what is in its production queue, and your homeworld's queue is empty.

In the **Production** tile, choose **Change**. Pick **Auto Factories** in the left list and press **Add ->**, then do the same with **Auto Mines**. Choose **OK** when you're done.

Factories make the resources everything is paid with; mines dig up the minerals.
tutorial.queue.title: Put your planet to work
tutorial.research.text:
Your scientists need a goal. Open **Commands > Research** ({key:research}), pick a field to study, and set how much of your resources goes to research. **Propulsion** gets your ships further; **Biotechnology** helps you settle more worlds.

Choose **Done** to close the window.
tutorial.research.title: Research
tutorial.scout.text:
You know almost nothing about the stars around you. Your two scouts can change that.

Click the **Wayfarer** by your homeworld to select it (click again to step through the fleets there). Then hold **Shift** and click a planet some way off: that adds a waypoint, and the scout will fly there.
tutorial.scout.title: Explore
tutorial.select_home.text:
Your race starts on a single planet, its homeworld. It's selected now: the planet in your colour, with your fleets beside it.

Its details are in the tiles on the left, and a summary at the bottom right. Clicking a planet or fleet on the map selects it; clicking your homeworld brings you back to it.

Choose **Next** when you're ready.
tutorial.select_home.title: Your homeworld
tutorial.welcome.text:
This tutorial walks you through your first years as the leader of a young race. Each step says what to do, and moves on by itself once you've done it.

You can hide the tutorial whenever you like. The help ({key:help}) explains everything in more detail.
